\begin{bankq}[id=SI12-P1-PHY-S1-Q06, source={Score-I - Test 12 (09 Mar 2022)}, paper=1, qno=6, type=multi, subtopic={Torque}, answer={A,B}, answer_src=key, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K2 S2 I0 C0 F1}, diff_note={concepts: rolling of a spool, torque and force equations | steps: constraint a = alpha r about the contact thread; force equation along the incline; torque equation; solve a and T}]
A spool of mass $m$ and moment of inertia $I$ about its axis rests on a smooth inclined plane, inclined at an angle $\theta$. The end of the thread is tied as shown. The outer radius of the spool is $R$ \& inner radius of the spool is $r$:
\bfig{98.0}{SI12_p1_phy_s1_q06_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Acceleration of centre of mass of spool $a_{cm}=\dfrac{mg\sin\theta}{m+\frac{I}{r^2}}$}
\opt{B}{Tension in thread is $T=\dfrac{mgI\sin\theta}{I+mr^2}$}
\opt{C}{Angular acceleration of spool is $\alpha=\dfrac{a_{cm}}{R}$}
\opt{D}{Acceleration of centre of mass is zero.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

A light stick of length $\ell$ rests with its one end against the smooth wall and other end against the smooth horizontal floor as shown in the figure. \bfig{110.4}{SA01_p2_phy_s1_q02_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$\mathrm a_P=\dfrac g{\sin\theta}\left(1-\dfrac x\ell\right)$}
\opt{B}{$\mathrm a_P=\dfrac g{\cos\theta}\left(1-\dfrac x\ell\right)$}
\opt{C}{The time taken by the bug to reach the bottom of the stick having started at the top end from rest is $\dfrac\pi2\sqrt{\dfrac{\ell\sin\theta}{3g}}$ .}
\opt{D}{The time taken by the bug to reach the bottom of the stick having started at the top end from rest is $\dfrac\pi2\sqrt{\dfrac{\ell\sin\theta}{g}}$ .}
\end{qoptions}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=TMAS02-P2-PHY-S3-G3-4, source={TMAS - Test 02 (06 Aug 2023)}, questions={3-4}]
The governing equation $\vec\tau=\dfrac{d\vec L}{dt}$, for rigid body motion bears formal resemblance to the translational equation $\vec F=\dfrac{d\vec P}{dt}$ where linear momentum $\vec P=M\vec v$ always holds true as $M$ does not have only directional value. On the other hand for rotational about fixed axis writing $\vec L=I\vec\omega$ can not be correct as $I$ has orientational value for rotation of a rigid body about a fixed axis, angular momentum can still be written as $\vec L=I_{xx}\vec\omega_x+I_{yy}\vec\omega_y+I_{zz}\vec\omega_z$ about three mutually perpendicular axes if there axes are symmetrical with respect to body. Symmetry we mean that with chosen coordinates axes $\sum m_ix_iy_i,\ \sum m_iy_iz_i\ \&\ \sum m_ix_iz_i$ are all zero.\par
Such axes are called principal axes. For a body with cylinderical symmetry, axis of revolution is a principal axis and other two principal axes are mutually perpendicular and lie in a plane through centre of mass, perpendicular to axis of rotation. Kinetic energy in pure rotation can then be written as\par\noindent\hfill{\small$K=\dfrac12I_{xx}\omega_x^2+\dfrac12I_{yy}\omega_y^2+\dfrac12I_{zz}\omega_z^2$}\hfill\null\par
The normal to a uniform ring of mass $2.5$ kg and radius $1$ m is making an angle $\theta=45^\circ$ with the vertical axis passing through is centre. The ring is rotating with angular speed $\omega=\sqrt{\dfrac25}$ rad/s about the vertical axis as shown.
\bfig{68.8}{TMAS02_p2_phy_s3_para3_4_1.png}
\end{bankpassage}
